meta.title: Solar astrophysics | LASCE
meta.description: Learn how LASCE studies solar activity, the Sun-Earth relationship and its effects on the space environment from Costa Rica.

hero.title: Solar astrophysics
hero.introduction: Solar activity does not end at the Sun. Its magnetic fields, its radiation and the stream of particles it releases extend across the Solar System and can change the space environment of the Earth.

overview.title: What does solar astrophysics study?
overview.intro: This area seeks to understand the physical processes behind the Sun's activity and to explain how those variations connect with the interplanetary medium and the Earth's environment.

activity.title: Solar activity
activity.description: It analyses eruptive phenomena such as flares, coronal mass ejections and solar radio emissions.

magneticField.title: Magnetic field
magneticField.description: It studies how magnetic fields store energy, structure the solar atmosphere and take part in eruptive events.

sunEarth.title: Sun-Earth relationship
sunEarth.description: It relates solar disturbances to the solar wind, the interplanetary magnetic field and the ionosphere.

analysis.title: Scientific analysis
analysis.description: It brings together observations, satellite data, ground stations and computational processing tools.

flow.title: Chain of study
flow.caption: LASCE connects data, models and analysis methods to study solar activity and its possible effects on the Earth and on technology.

meta.title: Space weather | LASCE
meta.description: What space weather is, how it relates to solar activity and why it is studied from Costa Rica at the Space Sciences Laboratory of the University of Costa Rica.

definition.title: What is space weather?
definition.p1: Space weather describes the changing conditions of the Sun, the solar wind and the ionosphere that can influence the Earth's surroundings and technological systems. It is not everyday atmospheric weather: it originates mainly in solar activity and shows itself in the space environment of our planet.

sunToEarth.title: From the Sun to the Earth

release.title: The Sun releases energy
release.description: Flares produce intense increases in radiation and are associated with the origin of coronal mass ejections (CMEs), which are large structures of plasma and magnetic field. Some of these events accelerate particles to high energies.

propagation.title: The disturbance propagates
propagation.description: Electromagnetic radiation arrives in about eight minutes, while particles and CMEs travel through the interplanetary medium on scales of minutes and of hours to days, respectively.

response.title: The Earth's environment responds
response.description: If the disturbance reaches the Earth under the right conditions, it can produce geomagnetic storms or ionospheric disturbances.

technology.title: Technology can be affected
technology.description: Sensitive systems include radio communications, GNSS navigation, satellites, power grids, and space and aviation operations.

costaRica.title: Why study it from Costa Rica?
costaRica.p1: The response of the ionosphere and the performance of technological systems can depend on geographic and geomagnetic location. Having observations and analyses made from Costa Rica makes it possible to characterise the regional environment better, to contribute data to global networks and to build local scientific capabilities. For a country that depends more and more on satellite navigation, telecommunications and digital infrastructure, understanding space weather is an investment in knowledge.

components.title: What makes up space weather?
components.intro: It is not a single phenomenon: it is a chain that starts at the Sun and ends at the Earth. Each link changes the next one.

solarActivity.title: Solar activity
solarActivity.description: The Sun is not still. Sunspots, flares and coronal mass ejections release energy, particles and magnetic fields into space.

solarWind.title: Solar wind
solarWind.description: It is a continuous stream of plasma leaving the solar corona. Its speed, density and magnetic field change according to what happens on the Sun.

magnetosphere.title: Magnetosphere
magnetosphere.description: The Earth's magnetic field deflects most of the solar wind. When that stream intensifies, the magnetosphere is compressed and can be disturbed.

ionosphere.title: Ionosphere
ionosphere.description: It is the upper layer of the atmosphere, ionised by solar radiation. Changes in that layer affect radio, GPS and other communications.

storms.title: Geomagnetic storms
storms.description: They arise when the solar wind and the interplanetary magnetic field strongly disturb the magnetosphere. They can last hours or days.

particles.title: Particle radiation
particles.description: The Sun can also send protons and other energetic particles. That stream is different from the everyday solar wind and can affect satellites and polar flights.

flow.title: Conceptual flow
flow.caption: The Sun's activity feeds the solar wind; that stream strikes the magnetosphere and, from there, effects appear on the Earth.

initiatives.title: International initiatives LASCE is part of

iswi.title: International Space Weather Initiative (ISWI)
iswi.logoAlt: Logo of the International Space Weather Initiative (ISWI)
iswi.p1: The International Space Weather Initiative (ISWI) of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space was launched in 2009 and formally concluded as an item on the Committee's agenda in 2012. However, ISWI activities continued and, since 2013, they have been addressed under the new permanent agenda item on space weather of the Committee's Scientific and Technical Subcommittee.

ivia.title: Ibero-American VLBI Initiative (IVIA)
ivia.logoAlt: Logo of the Ibero-American VLBI Initiative (IVIA)
ivia.p1: The Ibero-American VLBI Initiative (IVIA) emerged in 2019 as a joint working body aimed at developing radio astronomy in Ibero-America. Its guiding ideas are the development of radio astronomy in the region and the implementation of a VLBI network in Latin America, in collaboration with Spain and Portugal.
ivia.p2: It currently includes representatives of institutions from Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Mexico, Peru and Uruguay, and it aims to promote the participation of the other countries in the region. The Joint Institute for VLBI (JIVE, based in the Netherlands, the organisation that centralises data processing for the European VLBI Network, EVN), the Instituto Geográfico Nacional of Spain and the Instituto de Telecomunicações of Portugal also take part.
ivia.p3: The initiative involves collaborative work on converting telecommunication antennas into radio telescopes and adapting them for VLBI, and on developing all the related technologies. By pooling the resources of the participating institutions, it aims to reach a critical mass that makes the most of the resources and infrastructure existing in each country.
ivia.p4: The final goal is therefore to create an international collaboration project with a large impact on the overall development of the region.
ivia.p5: The initiative contributes strongly to narrowing the gap between the number of radio astronomy observatories in the Southern Hemisphere and those in the Northern Hemisphere.

machineLearningWorkshop.abstract: A workshop focused on the study of the Sun-Earth relationship, scientific data analysis and the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to space weather and GNSS systems.
machineLearningWorkshop.p1: As part of the LASCE project, the Workshop on Machine Learning Applied to Space Weather and Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) was held from 16 to 20 February 2026 in San José, Costa Rica. For five days the activity brought together students, early-career researchers and specialists to strengthen their skills in the study of the Sun-Earth relationship, scientific data analysis and the application of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques to space weather.
machineLearningWorkshop.p2: The programme combined lectures, discussion sessions and computational practice devoted to ionospheric processes, the effects of space weather on GNSS systems, scientific computing and data analysis with machine learning tools. This approach made it possible to combine the physical understanding of solar and terrestrial phenomena with modern methods of processing, modelling and prediction, while also promoting the use of open data and reproducible procedures.
machineLearningWorkshop.p3: The workshop had 52 in-person participants from 17 countries; 37.2% were women and 70% came from developing countries. It was organised with the participation of the Space Research Center of the University of Costa Rica, the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, the International Committee on GNSS, COSPAR, INGV and SCOSTEP, together with contributions from the National University of Tucumán and the Abdus Salam International Centre for Theoretical Physics.
machineLearningWorkshop.p4: This activity strengthened the international profile of LASCE, widened its networks of scientific collaboration and contributed to building regional capabilities for researching, monitoring and predicting the effects of space weather on the ionosphere and on technological systems. It also created a space for identifying new scientific challenges, opportunities for cooperation and future initiatives that combine space weather physics with advanced data analysis tools.

meta.title: About us | LASCE
meta.description: The Solar Astrophysics and Space Weather Laboratory (LASCE), part of the Space Research Center (CINESPA) at the Universidad de Costa Rica: what it is and what it researches.

hero.title: About us
hero.lead: Solar Astrophysics and Space Weather Laboratory, part of the Space Research Center (CINESPA) at the Universidad de Costa Rica.

overview.title: Who are we?
overview.p1: The Solar Astrophysics and Space Weather Laboratory (LASCE) is a scientific initiative linked to the Space Research Center (CINESPA) of the Universidad de Costa Rica. It brings together solar astrophysics research, astronomical observations and computational development to study solar activity, its interaction with the interplanetary medium and the terrestrial environment.
overview.p2: LASCE starts from a simple but powerful idea: to understand space weather, you need to observe different links in the same chain, from the magnetic origin of a solar eruption to its manifestations in near-Earth space. For this reason, LASCE carries out scientific research that integrates data from different instruments, wavelengths and platforms.

contribution.title: Distinctive contribution
contribution.p1: LASCE aims for Costa Rica to be not only a user of international information, but also a producer of data, knowledge and solutions adapted to its location and its needs.

vision.title: Our vision
vision.p1: To establish in Costa Rica a regional reference for observing the Sun, studying the Sun-Earth relationship and developing tools for monitoring and predicting space weather. This vision combines scientific excellence, technology developed with national participation, international cooperation, talent training and public communication of science.
